meta.changes: We kept only laws in force, removed repealed laws, and grouped RAND's law categories into one plain-language status per state for six topics. RAND's statute citations and notes are shown unchanged.

policies.title: Background checks for private sales
policies.question: If you buy a gun from another private person (not a store), does state law require a background check?
policies.explain: Federal law already requires licensed gun dealers to run a background check. It does not require one when one private person sells to another. Some states add that requirement.

policies.title: Carrying a concealed handgun
policies.question: Do you need a permit to carry a hidden handgun in public?
policies.explain: Permitless states let adults who may legally own a gun carry it hidden without a permit. In shall-issue states you need a permit, and officials must give it to you if you meet the rules. In may-issue states, officials have more choice.

statuses.label: Permit needed; officials have some choice
Permit needed; given if you meet the rules

policies.title: Waiting periods
policies.question: After you buy a gun, do you have to wait some days before you can take it home?
policies.explain: There is no federal waiting period. Some states require one. In some other states you first need a permit to buy, which takes time to get.

statuses.label: No set wait, but a permit is needed first

policies.title: Minimum age to buy a rifle or shotgun
policies.question: How old do you have to be to buy a rifle or shotgun?
policies.explain: Federal law says licensed dealers may not sell handguns to anyone under 21, or rifles and shotguns to anyone under 18. Some states set their own minimum age. If a state law has a big exception, RAND records the lower age the exception allows.

policies.title: Red flag laws
policies.question: Can a court order guns to be taken away from someone who is a danger to themselves or others?
policies.explain: These laws are officially called extreme risk protection orders. A court decides whether a person is a serious risk, and can order their guns removed for a limited time. In some states only police can ask the court, while in others family members can ask too.

statuses.label: Yes; police and others (like family) can ask

policies.title: Safe storage and children
policies.question: Does state law say how guns must be stored to keep them away from children?
policies.explain: Some states require all guns to be stored safely. Others punish careless storage if a child could get the gun. Some only make it illegal to knowingly give a gun to a child.

statuses.label: Guns must always be stored safely
Penalty if careless storage lets a child get a gun
Only knowingly giving a gun to a child is illegal

evidence.category: carrying a concealed weapon (ccw): shall issue
evidence.note:
Connecticut's concealed-carry law is  ambiguous and subject to different interpretations. In 1969, Connecticut established a Handgun Review Board to minimize arbitrary denials of permit applications. Sources such as Grossman and Lee (2008), and Ayres and Donohue (2009) consider 1969 to be the year Connecticut became "shall issue" in practice. We ultimately agreed, but note that Vernick and Hepburn (2003) characterize the law as remaining "may issue," and the NRA characterizes Connecticut's law as "reasonable/discretionary issue."

On June 23, 2022, the Supreme Court ruled in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen that 
while Connecticut, Delaware, and Rhode Island have laws with discretionary criteria, because they “appear to operate like ‘shall issue’ jurisdictions” and are therefore not unconstitutional.  “Although Connecticut officials have discretion to deny a concealed-carry permit to anyone who is not a ‘suitable person,’ see Conn. Gen. Stat. §29–28(b), the ‘suitable person’ standard precludes permits only to those ‘individuals whose conduct has shown them to be lacking the essential character or temperament necessary to be entrusted with a weapon.’”  As such, the Bruen decision did not reqjuire any real changes in rules or operations of the permitting system, but is recorded here to reflect that the Supreme Court concluded that any discretionary elements of the states law that might be considered a feature of a “may issue” state, are not unconstitutional.

Indiana, like Connecticut, call their laws "Risk Based Firearm Removal Laws." The key difference is that risk based firearm removal laws are implemented when the subject of the removal order already owns a firearm. However, both laws also include prohibitions about possessing a firearm while the order is in effect, essentially creating a scenario where the subject of the order could not legally purchase a firearm. ERPO laws state that the order can be served even if the person does not already own a firearm.

Delaware's concealed-carry law is ambiguous and subject to different interpretations. 

On June 23, 2022, the Supreme Court ruled in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen that 
while Connecticut, Delaware, and Rhode Island have laws with discretionary criteria they “appear to operate like ‘shall issue’ jurisdictions” and are therefore not unconstitutional.  As such, this “law change” does not entail any real changes in rules or operations of the permitting system, but is recorded here to reflect that the Supreme Court concluded that any discretionary elements of the states law that might be considered a feature of a “may issue” state, are not unconstitutional. In the case of Deleware, the court stated in a footnote that although DE includes discretionary criteria: "the state has thus far processed 5,680 license applications and renewals in fiscal year 2022 and has denied only 112. See Del. Courts, Super. Ct., Carrying Concealed Deadly Weapon (June 9, 2022), https://courts.delaware.gov/ forms/download.aspx?ID=125408. Moreover, Delaware appears to have no licensing requirement for open carry." Neither of these explanations for why DE's law is constitutional bear on the question of whether DE allows discretion in the decision to award CCW permits, so we retain the "may issue" designation for this law.

evidence.note:
Maryland uses the same abbreviation for an ERPO but the name is slightly different as the state uses "protective" instead of "protection" order (Extreme Risk Protective Order). This law identifys a broad range of individuals who can file for an extreme risk protection order: (I) a physician, psychologist, clinical social worker, licensed clinical professional counselor, clinical nurse specialist in psychiatric and mental health nursing, psychiatric nurse practitioner, licensed clinical marriage or family therapist, or health officer or designee of a health officer who has examined the individual; (ii) a law enforcement officer; (iii) the spouse of the respondent; (iv) a cohabitant of the respondent; (v) a person related to the respondent by blood, marriage, or adoption; (vi) an individual who has a child in common with the respondent; (vii) a current dating or intimate partner of the respondent; or (viii) a current or former legal guardian of the respondent.

Note that Maryland has three types of orders. In addition to the ex parte and full orders, the State also specifies an interim order that can be requested from judicial commissioners when the court is closed.

evidence.note:
According to documentation relied upon by Aneja, Donohue, and Zhang (2013), "Concealed carry banned until 2001 law, which was supposed to give out permits January 1st, 2002 (Law 2001, volume 2, page 1889).
